t: Tartessos was the first entity in south-western Iberia recognised as a kingdom, and Herodotus names its king Arganthonios as the host of the first Greeks to reach Iberia.
Its wealth lay in metals: by the Late Bronze Age silver extraction in Huelva Province had reached industrial proportions.
Scholars describe it as a hybrid archaeological culture, formed around the 9th century BCE through contact between Phoenician settlers and local people.
dyk: Excavations on two adjoining lots in the centre of Huelva, together 2,150 square metres, yielded some 90,000 fragments of local, Phoenician and Greek pottery dated from the 10th to the early 8th centuries BCE.
ev: Huelva becomes a manufacturing and trading harbour receiving goods from distant places
Phoenicians settle in Iberia and build their own harbour at Gadir
The Early Orientalizing phase begins, with the first imports from the eastern Mediterranean
The oldest known indigenous texts of Iberia are written in Tartessian in the Southwest script
A pebble mosaic is laid at Cástulo, the earliest recorded in Western Europe

f.homeland: Western Andalusia around the lower Guadalquivir (the ancient Baetis), Extremadura and southern Portugal; key sites Huelva, the Treasure of El Carambolo at Camas near Seville, La Joya, Medellín, Cástulo, Cancho Roano and Turuñuelo at Guareña
f.period: Pattern-burnished and "Carambolo" wares from the 9th to the 6th centuries BCE; an Early Orientalizing phase from c. 750 BCE; an orientalising phase c. 750–550 BCE; most sites abandoned in the 5th century BCE, after which the Classic Iberian culture took its place
f.known: wealth in tin, silver, gold and copper; trade with the Phoenicians of Gadir and with Greek Phocaeans; the Southwest script; King Arganthonios; the gold Treasure of El Carambolo; the earliest mosaic recorded in Western Europe, at Cástulo
f.sources: Greek and Roman writers including Herodotus, Ephorus, Aristotle, Strabo, Pausanias, Pliny the Elder and Appian; Adolf Schulten's work published in 1922; excavations at El Carambolo from 1958, at Huelva and at Turuñuelo from 2015; carbon-14 dating by the University of Groningen; about 97 inscriptions in the Southwest script
